sentence: Which interpretation preserves the timing of the discussion?
setupText: An applicant writes, 'Not until the final interview did the panel discuss salary.'
taskText: Which interpretation preserves the timing of the discussion?
text: An applicant writes, 'Not until the final interview did the panel discuss salary.' Which interpretation preserves the timing of the discussion?
options: Salary had already been discussed before the final interview.
Salary was discussed before every interview except the final one.
Salary first came up during the final interview.
Salary remained undiscussed throughout the final interview.
answer: Salary first came up during the final interview.
explanation: The fronted not-until phrase delays the discussion to that interview.

rationales.Salary had already been discussed before: 'Not until' excludes the earlier discussion suggested here.
rationales.Salary was discussed before every interv: The restriction concerns when discussion began, not an exception to repeated discussion.
rationales.Salary first came up during the final in: The fronted not-until phrase delays the discussion to that interview.
rationales.Salary remained undiscussed throughout t: The sentence locates the discussion at the final interview rather than beyond it.

sentence: Which rewrite preserves the meaning and requested order?
setupText: Rewrite 'A single survey rarely answers every question' with the frequency word first, using formal standard word order.
taskText: Which rewrite preserves the meaning and requested order?
text: Rewrite 'A single survey rarely answers every question' with the frequency word first, using formal standard word order. Which rewrite preserves the meaning and requested order?
options: Rarely a single survey answers every question.
A single survey does rarely answer every question.
Rarely does a survey answer more than one question.
Rarely does a single survey answer every question.
answer: Rarely does a single survey answer every question.
explanation: Fronted negative-frequency 'rarely' brings 'does' before the subject while leaving 'answer' in its base form.

rationales.Rarely does a single survey answer every: Fronted negative-frequency 'rarely' brings 'does' before the subject while leaving 'answer' in its base form.
rationales.Rarely a single survey answers every que: This lacks the auxiliary inversion required by the requested formal fronted pattern.
rationales.A single survey does rarely answer every: This can be grammatical but does not put the frequency word first.
rationales.Rarely does a survey answer more than on: This changes the claim from rarely answering all questions to rarely answering even two.

sentence: Which sentence meets that writing goal?
setupText: A report lists the rise in costs but gives no cause. Focus the missing explanation, not the fact that costs rose.
taskText: Which sentence meets that writing goal?
text: A report lists the rise in costs but gives no cause. Focus the missing explanation, not the fact that costs rose. Which sentence meets that writing goal?
options: What the report explains is why costs rose.
Why costs rose is explained in the report.
What the report does not explain is whether costs rose.
What the report does not explain is why costs rose.
answer: What the report does not explain is why costs rose.
explanation: The negative what-clause introduces the gap; the why-clause identifies the missing cause.

rationales.What the report explains is why costs ro: This turns the missing explanation into something the report provides.
rationales.Why costs rose is explained in the repor: This also claims the explanation is present.
rationales.What the report does not explain is whet: This questions the occurrence, which the setup says is established.
rationales.What the report does not explain is why: The negative what-clause introduces the gap; the why-clause identifies the missing cause.

sentence: Which cleft best preserves this contrast?
setupText: Applicants accepted the fee but complained that they had received very little warning. Highlight the cause of their complaint.
taskText: Which cleft best preserves this contrast?
text: Applicants accepted the fee but complained that they had received very little warning. Highlight the cause of their complaint. Which cleft best preserves this contrast?
options: It was the fee, not the late notice, that upset the applicants.
It was the late notice, not the fee, that upset the applicants.
It was the applicants, not the staff, that the late notice upset.
It was the late notice and the fee that upset the applicants.
answer: It was the late notice, not the fee, that upset the applicants.
explanation: The focused contrast identifies the notice as the cause and excludes the accepted fee.

rationales.It was the fee, not the late notice, tha: This reverses the source of dissatisfaction.
rationales.It was the late notice, not the fee, tha: The focused contrast identifies the notice as the cause and excludes the accepted fee.
rationales.It was the applicants, not the staff, th: This contrasts the affected people, not the possible causes, and adds an unsupported claim about staff.
rationales.It was the late notice and the fee that: This adds the fee to the complaint despite the stated acceptance.

sentence: What does this wording present as necessary?
setupText: A trainer says, 'Only by comparing both forms can you identify which fields have changed.'
taskText: What does this wording present as necessary?
text: A trainer says, 'Only by comparing both forms can you identify which fields have changed.' What does this wording present as necessary?
options: Identifying the fields before comparing the forms.
Comparing both forms in order to identify the changed fields.
Comparing whichever one form is easier to read.
Changing the fields before either form can be compared.
answer: Comparing both forms in order to identify the changed fields.
explanation: 'Only by' restricts the route to the stated result; comparison is presented as required.

rationales.Identifying the fields before comparing: This reverses the relation between the method and the result.
rationales.Comparing whichever one form is easier t: The necessary method explicitly includes both forms.
rationales.Comparing both forms in order to identif: 'Only by' restricts the route to the stated result; comparison is presented as required.
rationales.Changing the fields before either form c: The sentence concerns detecting existing changes, not making new ones.

sentence: 'The timetable became more flexible, and ___.'
setupText: The timetable became more flexible, and the payment rules became more flexible too. Shorten the second clause without changing that meaning.
taskText: 'The timetable became more flexible, and ___.'
text: The timetable became more flexible, and the payment rules became more flexible too. Shorten the second clause without changing that meaning. 'The timetable became more flexible, and ___.'
options: so did the payment rules
so were the payment rules
so the payment rules did
neither did the payment rules
answer: so did the payment rules
focusKey: coverage-inversion-and-emphasis-b2-1746:Ellipsis preserves an event rather than a state
explanation: 'Did' substitutes for 'became more flexible' and the inverted order adds another subject.

rationales.so did the payment rules: 'Did' substitutes for 'became more flexible' and the inverted order adds another subject.
rationales.so were the payment rules: 'Were' gives a state rather than repeating the change expressed by 'became'.
rationales.so the payment rules did: This order confirms an earlier claim about the rules; it does not perform the requested additive comparison.
rationales.neither did the payment rules: 'Neither' would add a negative proposition, conflicting with the two positive changes.

sentence: Which revision fits the requested rule?
setupText: Turn 'Staff must never share passwords' into a formal rule beginning 'Under no circumstances'. Preserve the complete prohibition.
taskText: Which revision fits the requested rule?
text: Turn 'Staff must never share passwords' into a formal rule beginning 'Under no circumstances'. Preserve the complete prohibition. Which revision fits the requested rule?
options: Under some circumstances may staff share passwords.
Under no circumstances need staff share passwords.
Under no circumstances must staff refuse to share passwords.
Under no circumstances may staff share passwords.
answer: Under no circumstances may staff share passwords.
explanation: The fronted negative phrase plus inverted 'may' expresses that sharing is never permitted.

rationales.Under some circumstances may staff share: This introduces permitted exceptions and also uses unmotivated inversion after a positive phrase.
rationales.Under no circumstances need staff share: This removes an obligation to share rather than prohibiting sharing.
rationales.Under no circumstances must staff refuse: This prohibits refusal, reversing the rule's practical effect.
rationales.Under no circumstances may staff share p: The fronted negative phrase plus inverted 'may' expresses that sharing is never permitted.

sentence: Choose a rewrite that preserves the event order.
setupText: The manager checked the receipt, then approved the refund. Approval had not been given before the check. Front the time restriction in formal English.
taskText: Choose a rewrite that preserves the event order.
text: The manager checked the receipt, then approved the refund. Approval had not been given before the check. Front the time restriction in formal English. Choose a rewrite that preserves the event order.
options: Only after the manager had checked the receipt was the refund approved.
Only after the refund had been approved did the manager check the receipt.
Only after had the manager checked the receipt was the refund approved.
Only after the manager had checked the receipt the refund was approved.
answer: Only after the manager had checked the receipt was the refund approved.
explanation: The after-clause keeps ordinary order; the passive main clause begins 'was the refund'.

rationales.Only after the refund had been approved: This puts approval before the check, reversing the sequence.
rationales.Only after the manager had checked the r: The after-clause keeps ordinary order; the passive main clause begins 'was the refund'.
rationales.Only after had the manager checked the r: The subordinate after-clause should not invert; the main clause does.
rationales.Only after the manager had checked the r: This preserves the facts but omits the main-clause inversion requested by formal fronting.

sentence: Which revision preserves the focus and the reviewer's judgment?
setupText: A reviewer writes, 'It is the wording of the question that I find confusing, not its subject matter.'
taskText: Which revision preserves the focus and the reviewer's judgment?
text: A reviewer writes, 'It is the wording of the question that I find confusing, not its subject matter.' Which revision preserves the focus and the reviewer's judgment?
options: What I find confusing is how the question is worded, not what it is about.
What I find confusing is what the question is about, not how it is worded.
The question is confusing because its subject matter is unfamiliar.
What makes the wording confusing is the question's difficult subject matter.
answer: What I find confusing is how the question is worded, not what it is about.
explanation: The what-cleft retains the same object of criticism while changing the cleft form.

rationales.What I find confusing is what the questi: This reverses the contrast between wording and subject matter.
rationales.The question is confusing because its su: This invents an unfamiliar-topic explanation that the reviewer excludes.
rationales.What I find confusing is how the questio: The what-cleft retains the same object of criticism while changing the cleft form.
rationales.What makes the wording confusing is the: This attributes the wording problem to the subject matter, which the original contrast sets aside.

sentence: What does 'Little did they realize' suggest in this narrative?
setupText: The team booked the workshop for one afternoon. Little did they realize that the repairs would take a week.
taskText: What does 'Little did they realize' suggest in this narrative?
text: The team booked the workshop for one afternoon. Little did they realize that the repairs would take a week. What does 'Little did they realize' suggest in this narrative?
options: They had not appreciated how long the repairs would take.
They knew the repairs would take only a little time.
They understood the week-long delay and planned for it.
They discovered the true duration while making the booking.
answer: They had not appreciated how long the repairs would take.
explanation: Negative 'little' foregrounds their lack of awareness, which the afternoon booking illustrates.

rationales.They had not appreciated how long the re: Negative 'little' foregrounds their lack of awareness, which the afternoon booking illustrates.
rationales.They knew the repairs would take only a: Here 'little' limits their awareness, not the duration of the repairs.
rationales.They understood the week-long delay and: The short booking and negative 'little' point to inadequate awareness.
rationales.They discovered the true duration while: The narrative contrasts the brief booking with what they did not yet appreciate.

sentence: Which sentence is correctly formed for that goal?
setupText: A colleague dismisses reliability as irrelevant. You want to reject that view using a what-cleft with emphatic 'does'.
taskText: Which sentence is correctly formed for that goal?
text: A colleague dismisses reliability as irrelevant. You want to reject that view using a what-cleft with emphatic 'does'. Which sentence is correctly formed for that goal?
options: What does matter is whether is the evidence reliable.
What does matters is whether the evidence is reliable.
What does matter is whether the evidence is reliable.
What does matter it is whether the evidence is reliable.
answer: What does matter is whether the evidence is reliable.
explanation: Emphatic 'does' is possible in the subject what-clause; the embedded question retains statement order.

rationales.What does matter is whether is the evide: The embedded whether-clause requires 'the evidence is', not question inversion.
rationales.What does matter is whether the evidence: Emphatic 'does' is possible in the subject what-clause; the embedded question retains statement order.
rationales.What does matter it is whether the evide: The what-clause is already the subject of 'is'; the extra 'it' breaks this cleft.

sentence: Which repair places inversion in the correct clause?
setupText: A writer drafts: 'Only when did we check the totals the pattern became clear.' Keep the time restriction and repair the inversion.
taskText: Which repair places inversion in the correct clause?
text: A writer drafts: 'Only when did we check the totals the pattern became clear.' Keep the time restriction and repair the inversion. Which repair places inversion in the correct clause?
options: Only when did we check the totals did the pattern become clear.
Only when we checked the totals did the pattern become clear.
Only when we checked the totals the pattern became clear.
Only when we did checked the totals did the pattern become clear.
answer: Only when we checked the totals did the pattern become clear.
explanation: The when-clause uses ordinary order; the main clause places 'did' before its subject.

rationales.Only when did we check the totals did th: This still inverts the subordinate when-clause unnecessarily.
rationales.Only when we checked the totals the patt: This removes the erroneous inversion but fails to add the required formal main-clause inversion.
rationales.Only when we did checked the totals did: Emphatic 'did' in the time clause would require 'check', not 'checked'.
rationales.Only when we checked the totals did the: The when-clause uses ordinary order; the main clause places 'did' before its subject.

sentence: Which revision satisfies both instructions?
setupText: Attendance has improved and complaints have fallen. Begin with 'Not only' and keep the present perfect in both clauses.
taskText: Which revision satisfies both instructions?
text: Attendance has improved and complaints have fallen. Begin with 'Not only' and keep the present perfect in both clauses. Which revision satisfies both instructions?
options: Not only attendance has improved, but complaints have also fallen.
Not only has attendance improved, but have complaints also fallen.
Not only has attendance improved, but complaints have also fallen.
Not only did attendance improve, but complaints have also fallen.
answer: Not only has attendance improved, but complaints have also fallen.
explanation: The first fronted clause inverts 'has'; the clause after 'but' keeps ordinary subject-before-auxiliary order.

rationales.Not only has attendance improved, but co: The first fronted clause inverts 'has'; the clause after 'but' keeps ordinary subject-before-auxiliary order.
rationales.Not only attendance has improved, but co: The first clause lacks the inversion required after this fronted not-only phrase.
rationales.Not only has attendance improved, but ha: The second declarative clause does not inherit the first clause's inversion.
rationales.Not only did attendance improve, but com: This is possible English but changes the first clause from the requested present perfect to simple past.

sentence: Which revision best meets that goal?
setupText: A draft reads, 'In the appendix does the author acknowledge the limitation.' The writer wants an ordinary statement with mild emphasis on the acknowledgment, not a question.
taskText: Which revision best meets that goal?
text: A draft reads, 'In the appendix does the author acknowledge the limitation.' The writer wants an ordinary statement with mild emphasis on the acknowledgment, not a question. Which revision best meets that goal?
options: In the appendix, does the author acknowledge the limitation?
In the appendix, the author does acknowledge the limitation.
Only in the appendix does the author acknowledge the limitation.
In no appendix does the author acknowledge the limitation.
answer: In the appendix, the author does acknowledge the limitation.
explanation: A positive location phrase does not require auxiliary inversion; stressed 'does' can remain after the subject.

rationales.In the appendix, does the author acknowl: This asks a question instead of making the requested acknowledgment.
rationales.Only in the appendix does the author ack: This adds a restriction excluding other locations; the goal does not authorize that change.
rationales.In the appendix, the author does acknowl: A positive location phrase does not require auxiliary inversion; stressed 'does' can remain after the subject.
rationales.In no appendix does the author acknowled: This negates the acknowledgment rather than emphasizing it.

sentence: Which relationship does this construction express?
setupText: A report says, 'So confusing was the notice that several tenants called for clarification.'
taskText: Which relationship does this construction express?
text: A report says, 'So confusing was the notice that several tenants called for clarification.' Which relationship does this construction express?
options: The calls made an otherwise clear notice confusing.
The notice's degree of confusion led to the calls.
The tenants called despite finding the notice clear.
The tenants could call only if the notice was clear.
answer: The notice's degree of confusion led to the calls.
explanation: Fronted 'so confusing' emphasizes degree, and the that-clause gives its result.

rationales.The notice's degree of confusion led to: Fronted 'so confusing' emphasizes degree, and the that-clause gives its result.
rationales.The tenants called despite finding the n: The report links the calls to confusion rather than to an unexpected contrast.
rationales.The tenants could call only if the notic: This invents a condition and reverses the stated description.

sentence: Which sentence follows the requested structure?
setupText: Neither password worked. Keep 'Neither the old password nor the new code' as one subject phrase in a past-tense statement.
taskText: Which sentence follows the requested structure?
text: Neither password worked. Keep 'Neither the old password nor the new code' as one subject phrase in a past-tense statement. Which sentence follows the requested structure?
options: Neither did the old password nor the new code worked.
Neither the old password nor the new code did worked.
Neither the old password nor the new code worked.
Neither worked the old password nor the new code.
answer: Neither the old password nor the new code worked.
explanation: Here 'neither ... nor' joins parts of the subject; it does not introduce an inverted negative clause.

rationales.Neither did the old password nor the new: The coordinated subject does not trigger inversion, and 'did' would require 'work'.
rationales.Neither the old password nor the new cod: Emphatic 'did' cannot be followed by past-form 'worked'.
rationales.Neither worked the old password nor the: The requested coordinated subject belongs before its verb, not around it.
rationales.Neither the old password nor the new cod: Here 'neither ... nor' joins parts of the subject; it does not introduce an inverted negative clause.

sentence: How does the second clause relate to the first?
setupText: A planner writes, 'The schedule is not merely late; it is impossible to use.'
taskText: How does the second clause relate to the first?
text: A planner writes, 'The schedule is not merely late; it is impossible to use.' How does the second clause relate to the first?
options: It corrects the claim that the schedule is late.
It explains that lateness is the only problem.
It withdraws both criticisms as too strong.
It adds a more serious criticism without denying lateness.
answer: It adds a more serious criticism without denying lateness.
explanation: 'Not merely' accepts the first criticism as insufficient on its own and adds a stronger one.

rationales.It adds a more serious criticism without: 'Not merely' accepts the first criticism as insufficient on its own and adds a stronger one.
rationales.It corrects the claim that the schedule: 'Not merely late' does not deny that it is late.
rationales.It explains that lateness is the only pr: The second clause introduces a further problem beyond lateness.
rationales.It withdraws both criticisms as too stro: Neither clause signals a withdrawal or softening of the criticism.

sentence: What follows from this sentence alone?
setupText: A policy states, 'Only if the receipt is original will the office consider a refund.'
taskText: What follows from this sentence alone?
text: A policy states, 'Only if the receipt is original will the office consider a refund.' What follows from this sentence alone?
options: An original receipt is required for consideration, but does not guarantee payment.
Any original receipt guarantees that the office will pay a refund.
The office must consider a refund even with a copied receipt.
The office has already approved refunds for all original receipts.
answer: An original receipt is required for consideration, but does not guarantee payment.
explanation: The restriction concerns eligibility for consideration; it does not turn consideration into approval.

rationales.Any original receipt guarantees that the: 'Only if' marks a requirement, and 'consider' is not a promise to pay.
rationales.The office must consider a refund even w: This removes the necessary condition expressed by 'only if'.
rationales.An original receipt is required for cons: The restriction concerns eligibility for consideration; it does not turn consideration into approval.
rationales.The office has already approved refunds: The future-oriented rule reports no completed approvals.

sentence: Which rewrite preserves that reason contrast?
setupText: A witness's statement was not rejected because it was brief. It was rejected because it lacked dates. Focus the actual reason using an it-cleft.

text: A witness's statement was not rejected because it was brief. It was rejected because it lacked dates. Focus the actual reason using an it-cleft. Which rewrite preserves that reason contrast?

It was because the statement was brief that it was rejected.
It was the dates, rather than the statement, that were rejected.
It was because the statement lacked dates that it was rejected.
answer: It was because the statement lacked dates that it was rejected.
explanation: The because-clause is the cleft focus and supplies the reason for rejection.

rationales.It was because the statement was rejecte: This reverses the cause and the result.
rationales.It was because the statement lacked date: The because-clause is the cleft focus and supplies the reason for rejection.
rationales.It was because the statement was brief t: This selects the explicitly excluded explanation.
rationales.It was the dates, rather than the statem: This changes what was rejected instead of explaining the rejection.

sentence: Which reading is supported by 'no longer' here?
setupText: An announcement says, 'No longer can applications be submitted by email.'
taskText: Which reading is supported by 'no longer' here?
text: An announcement says, 'No longer can applications be submitted by email.' Which reading is supported by 'no longer' here?
options: Email submission will become available for the first time.
Email submission is available only for a shorter period.
Email submission was available before but is unavailable now.
Email applications currently take less time to submit.
answer: Email submission was available before but is unavailable now.
explanation: 'No longer' contrasts a previous possibility with its present absence; fronting gives it emphasis.

rationales.Email submission will become available f: 'No longer' marks an ending, not a new introduction.
rationales.Email submission is available only for a: The phrase changes availability, not the length of a submission period.
rationales.Email applications currently take less t: 'Longer' is part of the negative time expression, not a duration comparison here.
rationales.Email submission was available before bu: 'No longer' contrasts a previous possibility with its present absence; fronting gives it emphasis.
